definitions: C=arcctg is the inverse of cot on (0,pi), with domain R. Cot is odd, has period pi, is strictly decreasing on each (n*pi,(n+1)*pi), is undefined at n*pi and has zeros pi/2+n*pi. Cot'=-1/sin^2. n always ranges over all integers. Exact trigonometric values and elementary identities are proof tools, not imported lesson material.
input_limitation: The 14 selected definition blocks do not define arctg's branch. Set B(x)=pi/2-C(x), the tangent inverse in (-pi/2,pi/2). Any tangent inverse value is B(x)+k*pi; a continuous full inverse branch has constant k in Z. Conditional k=0 results are identified, never asserted as a supplied convention.

solutions.solution: 312=-48+2*180, so period 180 degrees gives cot(312)=cot(-48). Oddness gives cot(-48)=-cot(48). None of 312,-48,48 is a multiple of 180 degrees.
solutions.result: The equality holds on all displayed inputs.
solutions.domain: All displayed cotangent inputs are allowed.

solutions.solution: 17.3*pi=0.3*pi+17*pi, so integer periodicity gives the equality. Neither coefficient is an integer; neither input is a pole.
solutions.domain: 17.3*pi and 0.3*pi are allowed.

solutions.solution: -320=40-2*180; periodicity gives the equality directly. Neither angle is a multiple of 180 degrees.
solutions.domain: Both inputs are allowed.

solutions.solution: 6.4*pi=-0.6*pi+7*pi gives cot(6.4*pi)=cot(-0.6*pi). Oddness gives cot(-0.6*pi)=-cot(0.6*pi). All three coefficients are nonintegers.
solutions.domain: All three cotangent inputs are allowed.

solutions.solution: 7.5*pi=pi/2+7*pi. Periodicity reduces to pi/2, where cos=0 and sin=1; the seed zero-set rule also gives zero. Half-integer multiples of pi are not poles.
solutions.result: Both displayed cotangent values are zero.
solutions.domain: Both inputs are allowed.

solutions.task: Prove the decreasing cotangent-value chain for 5,15,31,45 degrees.
solutions.solution: 0<5<15<31<45<180, so all inputs belong to one open cotangent branch. Strict branchwise decrease reverses the input order, yielding cot(5)>cot(15)>cot(31)>cot(45). No asymptote is crossed.
solutions.result: The requested strict inequality chain holds.
solutions.domain: All four angles belong to (0,180 degrees).

solutions.task: Prove the cotangent-value chain for -4,-14,-28,-45 degrees.
solutions.solution: -180<-45<-28<-14<-4<0. Branchwise strict decrease gives cot(-45)>cot(-28)>cot(-14)>cot(-4), hence cot(-4)<cot(-14)<cot(-28)<cot(-45).
solutions.result: The requested strict inequality chain holds.
solutions.domain: All four angles belong to (-180,0 degrees).

solutions.solution: Cot decreases on (0,pi), with cot(pi/4)=1 and cot(pi/2)=0. Therefore t is in [pi/4+n*pi,pi/2+n*pi], n in Z. Both bounds are included and no pole occurs.
solutions.result: Union over all integers n of the closed intervals [pi/4+n*pi,pi/2+n*pi].
solutions.domain: t is not a multiple of pi; parameter families specify all circle points modulo 2*pi.
solutions.drawing_description: Under P_t=(cos t,sin t), mark the closed counterclockwise arc from (sqrt(2)/2,sqrt(2)/2) to (0,1) and its antipodal closed arc from (-sqrt(2)/2,-sqrt(2)/2) to (0,-1). Include four endpoints; mark no other arc.

solutions.solution: Let a=C(2) in (0,pi/2). Reflection gives C(-2)=pi-a. Decrease reverses the bounds, so t is in [a+n*pi,pi-a+n*pi], n in Z. Endpoints are included. Circle points obey |X|<=2|Y| with Y!=0.
solutions.result: Union over all integers n of [C(2)+n*pi,pi-C(2)+n*pi].
solutions.domain: No multiple of pi is in a listed interval.
solutions.drawing_description: Draw the closed upper arc from (2/sqrt(5),1/sqrt(5)) through (0,1) to (-2/sqrt(5),1/sqrt(5)), and its antipodal closed lower arc from (-2/sqrt(5),-1/sqrt(5)) through (0,-1) to (2/sqrt(5),-1/sqrt(5)). Include every endpoint.

solutions.task: Draw all unit-circle points satisfying cot(t)=1.5.
solutions.solution: X/Y=3/2 and X^2+Y^2=1 imply (X,Y)=+/- (3/sqrt(13),2/sqrt(13)). Y is nonzero. With a=C(3/2) in (0,pi/2), the complete parameter family is t=a+n*pi, n in Z.
solutions.result: Exactly two antipodal points; t=C(3/2)+n*pi, n in Z.
solutions.domain: Neither point has Y=0; no solution parameter is a multiple of pi.
solutions.drawing_description: Mark only (3/sqrt(13),2/sqrt(13)) in quadrant I and (-3/sqrt(13),-2/sqrt(13)) in quadrant III.

solutions.task: Draw all unit-circle points satisfying cot(t)=0.
solutions.solution: cos(t)=0 and sin(t)!=0 imply t=pi/2+n*pi, n in Z, corresponding to (0,1) and (0,-1).
solutions.result: Exactly (0,1) and (0,-1); t=pi/2+n*pi, n in Z.
solutions.domain: Zero and integer multiples of pi are excluded as angles.
solutions.drawing_description: Mark exactly the north and south points of the unit circle, both included; mark no arc and no east or west point.

solutions.domain: Inverse input sqrt(3) is real; inverse output must belong to (0,pi).

solutions.solution: cot(pi/3)=(1/2)/(sqrt(3)/2)=1/sqrt(3). pi/3 is in (0,pi), yielding the unique inverse value.

solutions.solution: Equal nonzero sine and cosine at pi/4 give cot(pi/4)=1. pi/4 is in (0,pi), where uniqueness applies.
solutions.domain: Inverse input 1 is real; output is in (0,pi).

solutions.solution: cot(pi/2)=0 and pi/2 lies in (0,pi), so C(0)=pi/2. The inverse is defined at zero; cotangent itself is not defined at angle zero.
solutions.domain: Inverse input zero is allowed; output zero is outside the inverse range.

solutions.solution: Reflection of the inverse branch gives C(-x)=pi-C(x). Thus C(-sqrt(3))=5*pi/6; direct cosine/sine there equals -sqrt(3). The angle -pi/6 is not in (0,pi).
solutions.domain: Inverse input is real; only the output in (0,pi) is accepted.

solutions.solution: C(-1)=pi-C(1)=pi-pi/4=3*pi/4. Direct cotangent there is -1; -pi/4 is outside the required range.
solutions.domain: Inverse input is real; output is in (0,pi).

solutions.solution: C(-1/sqrt(3))=pi-C(1/sqrt(3))=2*pi/3. Direct cosine/sine there is (-1/2)/(sqrt(3)/2)=-1/sqrt(3).
solutions.domain: Inverse input is real; output is in (0,pi).

solutions.solution: C(1)=pi/4. Tangent inverse values at 1 are pi/4+k*pi. Left equals right if k=0, is smaller if k>=1 and larger if k<=-1.
solutions.result: Central-branch answer '='; other branches change the comparison.
solutions.domain: All inputs are real; missing arctg normalization prevents fixing k.

solutions.domain: All inputs are real; k is not fixed by the seed.

solutions.task: Prove the two inverse derivative formulas using inverse differentiation.
solutions.solution: For a continuous inverse g of f with f'(g(y)) nonzero, write delta=g(y+h)-g(y). Its difference quotient is 1/[(f(g(y)+delta)-f(g(y)))/delta], giving g'=1/f'(g(y)). For cot on (0,pi), cot'(C(x))=-1/sin(C(x))^2 is finite and nonzero, so C'(x)=-sin(C(x))^2=-1/(1+cot(C(x))^2)=-1/(1+x^2). For a tangent inverse branch T(x)=pi/2-C(x)+k*pi, cos(T(x)) is nonzero. Quotient differentiation of sin/cos gives tan'=1/cos^2, so T'=cos(T(x))^2=1/(1+tan(T(x))^2)=1/(1+x^2). Equivalently T'=-C'. The constant integer branch shift disappears on differentiation.
solutions.result: arctg'(x)=1/(1+x^2) for any continuous differentiable full tangent inverse branch; arcctg'(x)=-1/(1+x^2).
solutions.domain: Every real x; inverse outputs avoid their forward-function poles. Subsection 112 is not read.

solutions.solution: T(x)=pi/2-C(x)+k*pi gives T+C=pi/2+k*pi directly. Alternatively 231 gives (T+C)'=0 on R, and evaluation at zero gives T(0)+C(0)=k*pi+pi/2. Thus the printed identity follows when k=0, but its exact constant is not fixed by the selected definitions.
solutions.result: General constant pi/2+k*pi; printed identity requires central-branch normalization.
solutions.domain: Every real x for a continuous full inverse branch; seed does not specify k.

solutions.task: Solve cot(x)=1 for all real x.
solutions.solution: The unique representative in (0,pi) is pi/4. Any allowed solution reduces modulo pi to it by injectivity; periodicity proves every x=pi/4+n*pi is a solution.
solutions.domain: x not in {n*pi:n in Z}; every listed solution avoids those poles.

solutions.task: Solve cot(x/2)=sqrt(3) for all real x.
solutions.solution: Set u=x/2. cot(u)=sqrt(3) gives u=pi/6+n*pi by inverse-branch uniqueness and periodicity. Multiply both the offset and period by two to get x=pi/3+2*n*pi. Substitution proves sufficiency, branch reduction necessity.
solutions.domain: x not in {2*n*pi:n in Z}; all listed solutions avoid those poles.

solutions.task: Solve cot(2*x)=1/sqrt(3) for all real x.
solutions.solution: Set u=2*x. cot(u)=1/sqrt(3) gives u=pi/3+n*pi. Divide offset and period by two: x=pi/6+n*pi/2. Substitution gives cot(pi/3+n*pi)=1/sqrt(3); reduction and injectivity show no other solutions.
solutions.domain: x not in {n*pi/2:n in Z}; no listed offset is a pole modulo pi/2.

solutions.task: Solve cot(3*x)=3.5 for all real x.
solutions.solution: Let a=C(7/2). The selected inverse definition gives a unique a in (0,pi); decrease and 7/2>1 sharpen this to 0<a<pi/4. The equation is 3*x=a+n*pi, so x=a/3+n*pi/3. Substitution and branch reduction prove sufficiency and necessity.
solutions.domain: x not in {n*pi/3:n in Z}; 0<C(7/2)/3<pi/12 ensures no listed solution is a pole.

solutions.task: Solve cot(x/5)=0 for all real x.
solutions.solution: Set u=x/5. The seed's full zero set gives u=pi/2+n*pi. Multiplying the whole family by five yields x=5*pi/2+5*n*pi. Substitution gives cosine zero and sine nonzero; the complete zero-set rule proves necessity.
solutions.domain: x not in {5*n*pi:n in Z}; every listed solution is a half-period from a pole.
